children: , the enterprise-software and cloud-infrastructure giant, slid approximately 2.2% to $158.19 Thursday before its scheduled after-hours results. The stock's retreat put a spotlight on a much bigger question: how much debt can the AI boom absorb? U.S. hyperscalers have issued roughly $220 billion of debt over the past year.

Reuters Open Interest highlighted an unusual gap between two Oracle bonds due in 2055. A newer $3.5 billion issue yielded 7.86% on August 21, compared with 7.67% for an older $1 billion bond carrying similar seniority and redemption terms. The larger issue also traded with an option-adjusted spread that was 22 basis points wider. That runs against the normal playbook, where bigger bonds typically enjoy stronger liquidity and cheaper financing.

Oracle's annual filing explains why credit investors are demanding a closer look. Fiscal 2026 capital expenditures reached approximately $55.7 billion, exceeding operating cash flow by roughly $23.7 billion, while management later projected up to $95 billion of spending for fiscal 2027. The chart shows Oracle trading 18.92% below its $195.10 GF Value estimate, suggesting meaningful upside if its $638 billion backlog converts into cash quickly enough. The opportunity is enormous, but the bond market is warning that building the required AI capacity will not come cheaply.

title: Oracle Drops Over 2% as Its AI Debt Starts Breaking Bond Math
